Topic: If the knowledge dispersed among millions of individuals can never be gathered into any single planning committee, by what right and by what means can a democratic majority claim the competence to direct the economic life of a nation?
Machiavelli — Judgement:
Hayek's question is one I would put to any prince who thinks himself wise: no single mind holds the scattered knowledge of a whole people, so by what title does anyone, even a majority, command their livelihoods?

The question assumes that authority rests on competence, but I never found it so. A majority rules by force of numbers and by the habits of obedience it can maintain, not by knowing what a baker in Naples or a wool-merchant in Florence knows. What matters is that the people's goodwill is kept and their ruin avoided. A republic that plans everything will soon be hated for each failure, and a hated government does not last. I advised princes to leave men's property and women alone, since men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of an inheritance.

A democratic majority has no right to direct a nation's economic life, and it has no competence to do so. It may lawfully keep order, defend the state and hold the public purse, and nothing more without courting disaster.

*The state that commands every trade will be blamed for every hunger.*
Thomas Paine — Judgement:
Hayek's question is a fair one, and it lands on a system I would have condemned long before he named it: you ask by what right a majority governs what no mind can survey. I ask first what the "nation" is that the committee claims to plan.

A majority's right extends to securing every person's equal liberty, not to commanding their livelihoods. In *Agrarian Justice* I asked that society honour a common debt to the poor, and I did so by a plain, rule-bound endowment that leaves each person free to use their own knowledge. It did not call for a planning board. Commerce, I argued in *Rights of Man*, is "a pacific system, operating to unite mankind by rendering nations, as well as individuals, useful to each other." The dispersed knowledge you describe is the labour of free people, and no assembly can legislate it into being.

A majority holds no right to direct the economic life of a nation; its right is to guarantee the equal freedom, the common security and the just inheritance within which millions of free people direct it for themselves.

*Government may set the table and keep the peace, but it cannot know what each person hungers for.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Hayek's question assumes that a majority's authority rests on its competence, but I never grounded sovereignty in knowledge. It rests in fear: men flee the war of every man against every man by laying down their right to all things, and no calculation of prices enters the bargain.

The majority holds its right by covenant, not by wisdom. The sovereign need not know what a thousand tradesmen know; it need only keep the peace in which they trade, and such "competence" as the majority claims over commerce is usurpation, the pretence that authority to judge the commonwealth's safety extends to every bargain within it. Yet I never made the sovereign's rule bend to the subject's cleverness: where the law is silent, the subject is free, and that silence is the true province of economic life.

A democratic majority has the right to secure the peace and enforce the contracts, but it has no competence, and therefore no just claim, to direct the nation's economy.

*Authority is bought with obedience, not with knowledge; and a sovereign who mistakes the one for the other soon has neither.*
Keynes — Judgement:
Hayek's point about dispersed knowledge is a strong one, and I concede it. But he has proved only that no committee can *calculate* an economy, not that a democracy has no business *steering* one. The question runs together two things: managing the details of production and answering for the aggregate.

Millions of private decisions never add up to full employment on their own. Investment depends on expectations of an uncertain future, and when those collapse, no amount of local knowledge brings the unemployed back to work. The majority has no right to decide what shall be made, or by whom. It does have a duty, and the means, to keep total demand high enough that the dispersed knowers can use what they know. Those means are interest rates, public investment and the budget. The state need not know your business. It must see that the whole economy does not stall.

Democratic majorities are competent at the macro level and incompetent at the micro level, and they should govern only the former.

*The state must mind the level of the whole, and leave the choosing of the parts to those who know them.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
You ask whether numbers can stand in for knowledge that no assembly can hold. I ask the older question: may any power, royal or popular, govern by will what only reason can justify?

A majority that claims to direct every livelihood is the throne wearing a cap of liberty, still asserting that authority, not understanding, makes right. Yet reason is not idle in public life. Dependence corrupts judgement, whether it is the labourer's before the landlord or the woman's before her husband. A people may rightly abolish it through education, open property, and laws that bind every rank alike. It may secure the conditions under which each person reasons for themselves, but it may not do their reasoning for them.

A democratic majority has no right to command the nation's economy, only the duty to give every citizen the independence and education to conduct their own.

*Power may open the door to reason, but when it walks through on everyone's behalf, it has already shut it.*
